common_name: Little Cuties Coco Loco Heuchera (Improved Miniature Chocolate Coral Bells)

planting.note: Set container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil; this Terra Nova Nurseries release improves on the older 'Little Cuties Coco' with a tidier habit and a longer bloom run.

directions: Coco Loco is a dwarf coral bells bred as a refinement of the earlier 'Little Cuties Coco', keeping the same silky, scaled-down chocolate-brown foliage but adding a fuller mound and a noticeably longer run of pink-and-white flower spikes from late spring into fall. Its tiny proportions keep the plant perfectly in scale for mixed containers, trough gardens, and the front edge of a shaded bed where a standard heuchera would overwhelm its neighbors. Give it evenly moist, well-drained soil and part shade for the richest leaf color, though it tolerates considerably more sun than most dark-leaved heucheras. Divide congested crowns every two to three years in spring to keep the mound tight.
sources: terranovanurseries.com -- Heuchera LITTLE CUTIES 'Coco Loco' product page

common_name: NOVA Brilliant Swedish Ivy (White-Edged Trailing Plectranthus)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after last frost into containers or hanging baskets; this Terra Nova release is grown outdoors as a tender annual foliage plant outside zones 9-11.

directions: NOVA Brilliant is an improved, thicker-leaved trailing Plectranthus with deep emerald-green leaf centers framed by a broad, bright white margin, grown mainly for its dense, self-branching mound of variegated foliage rather than its small blue-purple flowers in early fall. It holds a more upright, filled-in habit than older trailing selections, making it useful spilling over the edge of mixed baskets and patio containers or grown as a houseplant through winter. Site it in part to full shade, since the thin white leaf margin can scorch in strong sun, and keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged. Pinch tips occasionally to keep the trailing stems branching and full.

common_name: Peter Pancake Voodoo Lily (Compact Hybrid Amorphophallus)

planting.note: Plant the bare-root tuber after the soil has warmed in spring in rich, well-drained soil; this Plant Delights hybrid (A. dunnii x henryi) dies back in winter and resprouts in spring from its underground tuber.

directions: Peter Pancake is a hybrid aroid in the Amorphophallus dunryi grex, sending up a single mottled petiole each spring that unfurls into one broad, deeply divided compound leaf resembling a tropical umbrella. Like its relatives it dies to the tuber each winter and needs a dry dormant rest before resprouting the following spring. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade, siting it where the bold summer foliage display can be appreciated as a specimen or container accent. Avoid overwatering while dormant, since the tuber is prone to rot in cold, soggy soil.

common_name: Sound of Music Hosta (Large Wavy-Margined Patented Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to shade; this patented (US PP 35,563) Hans Hansen/Walters Gardens hosta builds into a substantial, winter-dormant mound.

directions: Sound of Music is a large-scale, patented hosta release bred by Hans Hansen for Walters Gardens, reaching about 30 inches tall and forming a substantial clump suited to anchoring a shaded bed or woodland planting rather than edging a path. Grow it in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to full shade, protecting the foliage from hot midday exposure to keep the leaf margins from scorching. Established clumps send up scapes of the typical lavender hosta flowers in summer, drawing hummingbirds. Divide only when the center of the clump becomes crowded, since large hostas like this one build slowly and resent frequent disturbance.

common_name: Wollaston's Soft Shield Fern (Heat-Tolerant Bulbil Fern)

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring in average garden soil in part sun to light shade; this historic 1852 Devon hedgerow find (G. Wollaston) shows notably better heat tolerance than many soft shield fern selections.

directions: Wollaston is a finely dissected, lacy-fronded form of the soft shield fern, originally found growing wild in an English hedgerow in 1852 and distinguished from plain 'Proliferum' by sturdier performance in hot summers. Like other Divisilobum-group selections it produces small bulbils along the frond midribs that can be pegged onto moist compost to raise new plants without disturbing the parent clump. Grow it in average, well-drained garden soil in part sun to light shade, leaving the evergreen fronds in place over winter to protect the crown. It adapts well to rock gardens, shaded walls, and woodland borders where its soft texture contrasts with bolder-leaved shade perennials.
sources: plantdelights.com -- Polystichum setiferum 'Proliferum Wollaston' product page

common_name: Caribbean Star Hardy Begonia (Silver Jagged-Leaf Fall-Blooming Begonia)

planting.note: Set out container divisions after frost danger has passed in humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade; this Tim Anderson hybrid has survived outdoors to about 11F at Juniper Level Botanic Garden but is safest as a container or houseplant in colder zones.

directions: Caribbean Star is a hardy begonia hybrid bred by Tim Anderson of Palm Hammock Orchid Estate, grown chiefly for its large, hand-sized leaves -- silvery gray with jagged edges and contrasting green veins -- rather than its modest stalks of pink flowers, which appear in fall as the plant's main bloom display. It dies back to the ground in winter wherever hard freezes occur and resprouts from its rhizome in spring, though in regions colder than about zone 8 it is better treated as a container or indoor plant brought in before frost. Grow it in light shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, and expect hummingbirds and butterflies to visit the fall flowers. Its patterned foliage makes a striking textural accent in a shaded cottage-style planting.

common_name: Silver Arrow Italian Arum (Silver-Centered Winter-Foliage Arum)

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall in well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; foliage emerges in autumn, persists through winter, and the plant goes dormant again by summer, a reverse growth cycle from most perennials.

directions: Silver Arrow is a 2003 seedling selection of Italian arum notable for arrow-shaped leaves with a dark green central ridge and border enclosing a large, contrasting silver patch across most of the blade. Leaves emerge in fall and remain the main ornamental feature through winter, since the plant is dormant through summer like other Italian arum forms, with inconspicuous spring flowers followed later by the species' typical orange berry spikes. Site it in part sun to light shade in well-drained soil, including dry shade under deciduous trees where little else performs well through the cool season. It is an easy, drought-tolerant filler for winter containers and makes an unusual groundcover where its reverse dormancy fills a seasonal gap.
sources: plantdelights.com -- Arum italicum 'Silver Arrow' product page
